title: Silicon Nanoparticles In Planta: Delivery Vehicle or Redox Primer?
content: Silicon nanoparticles (SiNPs) are widely reported to improve plant stress tolerance, yet the field has never settled on what the particle itself contributes. The simplest explanation is that SiNPs are a slow-release source of orthosilicic acid (Si(OH)4), and every benefit attributed to the nanoscale is a benefit of silicon delivery. We call this the dissolution-first null hypothesis and argue that most published studies cannot reject it. We then set out a competing model drawn from silica surface chemistry: amorphous silica surfaces carry silanols and strained siloxane rings that generate reactive oxygen species (ROS). On this view, a mild, surface-dependent redox pulse acts as a eustress signal that primes ROS, reactive nitrogen and sulfur species (RNS and RSS) networks, and the antioxidant upregulation reported across the literature is a downstream consequence rather than the mechanism. We outline where the two models diverge, highlight silicon non-accumulators as a revealing and neglected case, and propose a reporting standard so that future SiNP-plant studies can be interpreted mechanistically.
